title: Workflows and agents
description: Two ways to build a multi-step task: a workflow set in advance and an agent that works it out itself — and when to pick which.

steps.text: This is where the course turns a corner. The lessons behind you were about the model: what it sees in a request, what it counts with, why it makes mistakes, and why it remembers nothing between answers. That was the engine. From here on it's about everything built around it: who decides the next step, what the agent acts with, and what it's allowed to do. Remember how, in the lesson “What AI is and what an agent is,” I promised to come back to the parts one at a time? Here we are.

steps.imagePrompt: Two ways up the same mountain: a straight railway with fixed stations on one side, and a small explorer robot choosing its own trail with a compass on the other.
steps.caption: A workflow is a laid-out route; an agent picks its own path

steps.question: Two multi-step tasks: “read a document and translate it” and “find out why my bill went up.” Why are they built in fundamentally different ways?
steps.answer: The first one has a route known in advance — that's a workflow. The steps of the second only become clear along the way — that's a job for an agent.

steps.text: The first way is a workflow. It's a sequence of steps set in advance: the developer wrote down to do this first, then that, then this — the route is known ahead of time. Example: you send a photo of a document. Step 1 is to recognize the text, step 2 is to translate it, step 3 is to make a summary. Always the same steps in the same order, whatever you send.

What's good about a workflow: it's predictable and reliable, easier to debug, and cheaper, because there are no extra requests. The downside: it won't adapt to an unusual task. One step off the script and it's lost.

The second way is an agent. Here the model itself decides what to do next: which steps to take, which tools to call and when to stop. It lays out the route as it goes. Example: “gather what was written about the new law this week.” It's unclear in advance how many times to search or where to look. The agent decides: searched → not enough → narrowed it down → found it → put it together. Different every time.

What's good about an agent: it's flexible and handles tasks where there's no plan in advance. The downside is the other side of the same flexibility: it's less predictable, costs more (more requests and tokens), and is harder to debug.

A rough but accurate comparison. A workflow is rails: the train follows the set route, never turns off, and that's reliable. An agent is a driver: it picks the road to the goal, goes around a traffic jam, but might also get lost.

steps.caption: A workflow is rails, an agent is a driver
One task, two workers: run it on both tabs, then throw in a “Surprise”

steps.text: A common misconception: “an agent is always cooler and smarter.” No. For a clear, repeatable task, a workflow is usually better — faster, cheaper and with no surprises. You choose an agent not because it's “smarter” but because the task is unpredictable. Hence the rule of choice: the task is clear and repeats the same way — workflow; you don't know in advance how many steps there will be or which tools you'll need — agent.

In practice they are often combined: the overall frame is a workflow (reliable rails), and an agent works inside the single step that needs flexibility. By the way, you've already seen an agent at work with me: when I decide on my own to look at your calendar or set a reminder, that's agent behavior, and you can see it in the “Tool calls” panel (the wrench icon in the chat header).

steps.instruction: Match each approach to what it is:

pairs.def: The steps are set in advance — rails
Decides the next step itself — a driver
A frame of rails, with flexibility inside a step

steps.situation: Every morning you need the same summary: the weather in three cities and the exchange rate.
options: Workflow — the steps are known and repeat the same way
Agent — let it decide itself each time
A swarm of agents, one for each city
steps.explain: The task is clear and repeatable — rails are more reliable and cheaper than a driver.

steps.situation: The task: “find out why the channel's subscribers dropped this week and suggest what to do.”
options: Agent — it's unclear where to look or how many steps
Workflow — analytics always follows the same steps
Neither — this is a job for a person
steps.explain: Look at the statistics → spot something → dig deeper. The route is laid out as you go — an agent's profile.

steps.text: Practice. Think of two tasks: one strictly repeatable (“every morning, send me the list of the day's meetings”) and one with an unknown plan (“find out why my electricity bill went up”). Work out which is a workflow and which is an agent. This is exactly the fork developers face every time.

In short. Multi-step tasks are built in two ways. A workflow has set steps: predictable, reliable, cheap, but inflexible. An agent has the model choose the steps itself: flexible, but costlier and less predictable. A clear task → workflow, an unknown plan → agent, and they are often combined.

questions.q: How is an agent different from a workflow?
options: An agent picks its own steps, a workflow follows set ones
No difference — they're synonyms for one approach
An agent is always faster and cheaper than a workflow
questions.explain: A workflow has fixed steps; an agent decides its course itself.

questions.q: When is a workflow the better choice?
options: When the task is clear and repeats the same way
When the plan is unknown and changes along the way
Always — a workflow is simply better
questions.explain: A workflow is good for predictable, repeatable tasks.

questions.q: What is true about an agent?
options: Flexible, but costlier and less predictable
Always cheaper and more reliable than a workflow
Never makes a mistake in choosing steps
questions.explain: An agent's flexibility is both its plus and the reason for its higher cost and unpredictability.
